spots.name: St Peter's Basilica
spots.label: St Peter's Basilica

text.geographic_location: St Peter's Basilica stands in Vatican City, at the western end of St Peter's Square. It lies west of the River Tiber, near the Janiculum Hill.
text.directions_text: The nearest stop is the Risorgimento/S. Pietro tram stop (tram 19), about 9 minutes on foot from the basilica, which lies to the south-west of the stop. From the Metro, Cipro (Metro line A) is about 12 minutes on foot (the basilica lies to the south-east of the station) and Ottaviano (Metro line A) about 15 minutes (to the south-west). The phone icon on the map is about 290 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.description:
St Peter's Basilica is the great Renaissance church of Vatican City, and its central dome dominates the Rome skyline. The building is approached across St Peter's Square, which has two sections, an oval and then a trapezoid, both wrapped in tall colonnades. The wide façade, with its giant columns, stretches across the far end. Two statues of Saints Peter and Paul, each 5.55 metres tall, stand on the steps in front.

That is why it photographs so well. The colonnades lead the eye towards the façade, and the dome rises behind it as a clear finishing shape. Building work began on 18 April 1506 and finished on 18 November 1626, and several famous architects shaped the design, including Bramante, Michelangelo and Carlo Maderno. Bernini designed the square and many of the fittings. It is also the largest church in the world by interior measure.

The phone icon on the map is about 290 m east of the subject. At that distance the whole building fits in the frame with room for the open space and people in front of it. Take one wide shot to show the scale, then zoom in for the dome and the statues. Keep your phone level so the tall columns do not lean. If the square is busy, wait a moment for a gap, or use people walking across it to show how big the place is.
text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the basilica is a working place of worship, so check the official site before you go for entry and dress rules.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 290 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives warm light on the stone, but go early in the day if you want fewer people in the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the centre of the façade and dome with the middle vertical line. Use the horizontal lines to keep the rooftop level and the columns upright. Leave some open ground and people in the lower part of the picture to give a sense of scale. Then zoom in for a tighter shot of the dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the stonework. If you use telephoto, hold the phone steady with both hands and elbows tucked in.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole façade and dome together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the colonnades and the open square in the frame, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome and the statues on the steps.

spots.name: Michelangelo's Pietà
spots.label: Pietà

text.geographic_location: Inside St Peter's Basilica in Vatican City, in the first chapel on the north side just after the main entrance (about 41.9023, 12.4546).
text.directions_text: Start at the Risorgimento/S. Pietro stop on tram 19. The basilica is to the south-west, about 8 minutes on foot. From Cipro (Metro line A) it is about 13 minutes on foot, heading south-east. From Ottaviano (Metro line A) it is about 14 minutes on foot, heading south. Once inside the basilica, look for the first chapel on the north side after the entrance. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.description:
Michelangelo's Pietà shows Mary holding the body of Jesus after he has been taken down from the cross. It is carved from Carrara marble and dates from 1498–1499. It stands in St Peter's Basilica, in the first chapel on the north side after you come in, where it has been since the 18th century. It was made for a French cardinal's funeral chapel in the older church that stood on the site.

It photographs well because the whole group forms a calm pyramid, with Mary's head at the top and her wide, heavy drapery spreading out to the base. Mary looks very young, and the faces and folds of cloth are what draw the eye, so a close, simple frame suits it. It is also the only work Michelangelo ever signed. His name is carved on the sash across Mary's chest, though it is too small to read clearly in a phone photo from a distance.

The sculpture sits behind a bulletproof glass screen, which was replaced and updated in November 2024 ahead of the 2025 Jubilee. The screen can pick up reflections, so move a little to one side and watch for bright patches before you shoot. Take a few frames, then pick the sharpest. The basilica can be dimly lit and busy, so hold the phone steady with both hands and keep your elbows against your body.
text.access_note: This is a place of worship, and entry rules, dress code and any photography rules may apply, so check the official site before you go.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand as near the front of the chapel as is allowed, slightly off to one side rather than dead centre.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the basilica is quieter so you have a clear spot at the front of the chapel. Check the official site for visiting times.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the pyramid shape of the group in the middle, with Mary's head near the top of the frame. Keep the sculpture upright and avoid cutting off the base. For a second shot, go closer with telephoto on the faces and the folds of Mary's drapery.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the marble (the face of Jesus or Mary) to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white stone keeps its detail. Night mode can help in dim light, but hold very still, as it needs a steady phone. Check your photo for reflections in the glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the whole chapel, then try telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to fill the frame with the two figures. Because of the glass, telephoto lets you stay back and still get a close view. Ultra-wide (0.5x) is better kept for the basilica interior around it.

spots.name: Dome of St Peter's (rooftop view)
spots.label: St Peter's Dome

text.geographic_location: In Vatican City, at the middle of St Peter's Basilica, under its central dome, which stands at the end of St Peter's Square on the west side of the River Tiber. The basilica is close to the Janiculum Hill and Hadrian's Mausoleum.
text.directions_text: The nearest stop is the tram 19 stop Risorgimento/S. Pietro, about 9 minutes on foot from the phone icon on the map, with the dome lying to the south-west. Alternatively, take Metro line A to Cipro (about 12 minutes on foot, dome to the south-east) or to Ottaviano (about 15 minutes on foot, dome to the south-west). Once you reach St Peter's Square, the basilica and its dome are impossible to miss. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.description: The subject is the great dome of St Peter's Basilica, and the phone icon on the map sits right at it, so the picture here is the view looking out from the dome rather than a shot of it from the square. The dome is one of the largest in the world and dominates the Roman skyline, so from up here you look out over St Peter's Square, the rooftops of Rome and the city beyond. The square is a forecourt in two parts, an oval and a trapezoid, both ringed by tall colonnades. From above, that shape reads clearly and makes a strong, graphic foreground for a phone photo. The basilica was designed principally by Bramante, Michelangelo and Maderno, with the square and fittings by Bernini. Building began on 18 April 1506 and finished on 18 November 1626. That is more than a century of work behind the stonework around you. For phone photos, keep the horizon level and use the gridlines to line up the colonnades and rooflines. Tap on the distant skyline to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky looks washed out. If you are shooting through railings or a window, hold the lens close to the barrier and keep your hand steady. Take a few frames at different zoom levels, because the same view can look very different at 0.5x and at 3x. Expect to share the space with other visitors.
text.access_note: Access to the dome and any viewing level may be ticketed, timed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier or later in the day usually gives softer light and gentler shadows over the rooftops than midday sun. Check the official site for visiting times before you plan.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the horizon on the top or bottom third line. Use the curve of the colonnades as a leading shape and keep the lines straight. Take one wide shot, then a tighter zoomed shot of a single landmark. Take a few frames, since people move through the view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the distant rooftops to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly to keep the sky from burning out. If the view is hazy, a Live Photo can give you a choice of frames. Wipe your lens before you start.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the square, the colonnades and the sweep of Rome's rooftops. Use the default lens (1x) for a natural view. Use the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out distant domes and towers.
